📋 Oncology data overload? New study enrolling!

A single-center, prospective study of CME/IME providers navigating conference season. No placebo arm because weak oncology content is already doing that job.

Hypothesis: Clear, concise, and engaging content informs clinical practice. Revolutionary, I know – Copernicus is spinning in his grave.

Enrollment criteria:

·      Suffering through at least 1 CME deck that opened with a 47-bullet slide on KRAS mutation epidemiology – and then somehow got worse  
·      Documented exposure to MOA explained with 'vibes'
·      A content pipeline that exceeds your team's bandwidth

Intervention: Conference coverage & content development including slides, data summaries, blogs, tweetorials, decision aids, infographics, abstracts, and posters.

👉 Primary Endpoint: The guy in the back of the room finally puts his phone down.

Need support with #ESMO26 coverage, your next CME series, or the oncology content piling up in between? DMs are open.

IRB approval pending from my dog, Mitzi.

#Oncology #CME #IME #MedEd #MedicalWriting #Strategy

I've been running my LinkedIn "strategy" the way James Watt would have run his steam engine experiments if he'd also changed the coal type, piston size, ambient temperature, and the definition of 'steam' every single Tuesday.

Changing up posting days and times (often simultaneously), I've referenced medical news, metal detectors, kitchen recipes, Costco, and Socrates...and that was just the last 7 days. Earlier posts involved a tankless goldfish and a retriever reading Kant.

I've generated exactly zero actionable insights and approximately one confused algorithm.

What I DO have is a dataset that would make any scientist weep into their confidence intervals. 

The findings? Inconclusive. Would a control arm help? Larger sample size?

👉 Need oncology content for CME or other projects? Currently enrolling new clients - no randomization required.

My research assistant just handed me a small novel: "Here's everything I found!" 

Like an anxious PhD student, the AI shows all its work and every citation checks out, from PubMed URLs to clinical trial NCTs. Data points are all present and accounted for.

And yet, as usual, I ask: what's missing?

It's a kind of Socratic ritual where I'm the philosopher looking for the right questions. 

"Here's everything you should have asked" reveals my blind spots. A question I didn't consider, an assumption I left unchallenged. 

Unknown unknowns. In oncology, those often turn out to be the most important bit.

👉How do you find the gaps when everything looks perfect?

#AI #CME #MedEd #MedComms #Oncology

I went shopping for a case of AI getting oncology wrong. My LLM delivered the Costco version.

The task: show AI giving outdated breast cancer advice. Its pick? Recommending T-DM1 rather than T-DXd after THP for HER2+ mBC. 

"Gotcha," I thought. The FDA has moved on. T-DXd + pertuzumab was FDA-approved for frontline use 10 months ago. And the HER2CLIMB-05 maintenance regimen approved 2 weeks ago? Fuhgeddaboudit. 

Then I checked NCCN. THP is still category 1, preferred. T-DXd + pertuzumab is 'other recommended.' HER2CLIMB-05 isn't there yet.

The AI wasn't outdated. It was going by the book.

And there are valid reasons for the distinction. A big PFS gain, but immature OS. The 12% ILD rate. Continuous T-DXd dosing to intolerance/progression vs finite taxane followed by HP maintenance. And because DESTINY-Breast09 didn't allow crossover, nobody knows yet whether T-DXd up front is better than saving it for later. Especially now with tucatinib + HP maintenance.

'Approved' and 'preferred' run on different clocks. Good education explains the gap.

I went shopping for an AI mistake, but came home with a bulk pack of nuance.  

#AI #CME #MedEd #MedComms #BreastCancer #Oncology

Over 96% of med students use AI. 90% have personally caught it being wrong. Reassuring or apocalyptic? Depends on your risk tolerance.

In a late-2025 survey of 286 Canadian med students, AI tools most commonly included ChatGPT (93%) and OpenEvidence (58%). 

Only 2% said AI's never been wrong. Another 8% weren't sure. Let that marinate for a bit. 

Sour milk, old eggs, and the occasional hallucinated ingredient can ruin a recipe.

They can also ruin a patient.

Season with this: 55% had seen their instructors use AI-generated content, but only 11% were ever trained to use the tools. And barely a fifth understood enough about data privacy to know what they were handing over if they typed patient cases into a chatbot.

A whole generation of future clinicians is improvising in the kitchen and hoping dinner's edible. How do we train them to be top chefs?

#AI #CME #MedEd #MedComms

My AI oncology news scraper is like a metal detector on the beach. It just BEEPED a 'potential paradigm shift' for a phase 2 trial of 47 patients with a P-value of 0.049. The X post it found racks up another 40K impressions while I hunt for a clue in an obscure journal. 

There isn't one. To the AI, keyword volume + hype = BEEP. It can't tell 'barely significant' from 'clinically meaningful,' yet only one is worth digging up. It won't flag the outdated control arm as a coin someone buried themselves. 

The scraper's sensitivity dial remains unfazed by prompt engineering. Philosophically committed to the idea that all clinical trials are created equal. It's already beeping at a soda can: a single-center retrospective study of self-reported data.

Before I start digging, I check 3 things: trial design, effect size, and width of the confidence interval. 

The detector finds everything. Identifying the gold among the bottle caps is still the job.

It's ESMO season, and 10 of 12 Presidential abstracts report 'meeting primary endpoints.' Seven have declared a survival win, including the VOLGA trial now under priority review.

That's it, that's the whole thing.

No numbers or curves, just vibes and the word 'meaningful' doing the heaviest lifting in the English language since 'fine.'

We're in the era of conference movie trailers. Full Inception foghorn energy. BRAAAM. "One trial. One tumor type. This October...everything changes." 

And I'll still be first in line on opening night. Who's with me?

Every year, a certain breed of med-ed professional shows up to ASCO looking like they just heard about bispecific antibodies for the first time.

Scrambling. Commissioning slide decks at midnight. Asking their junior associate to "quickly wrangle" abstract libraries the size of a NYC phonebook while boarding a flight to Chicago.

What was missed? The top ASCO abstracts in a trenchcoat and mustache. Interim analyses at ASH, ESMO, SITC, AACR, SABCS, and WCLC that were skimmed and filed under "interesting, revisit later." 

Last December, I was building a daraxonrasib program. By ASCO26, RASolute-302 was the hottest topic in the room.

The lead investigators you'll see on every panel next June already know what they're going to be talking about. They started knowing around eighteen months ago.

Med-ed that matters is built before the invitations go out. 

Everything else is just printing lanyards for a party that's already in full swing.

#CME #MedEd #MedComms

I don't let AI write my oncology CME slides. I let it argue with them.

My slides get two final reviews before they ship. One by me. One by an AI that has absolutely zero interest in protecting my feelings or my reputation.

I build the slides myself, making sure every mechanism, trial finding, and nuance is solid. Then I pass them over to the AI like a prosecutor handing evidence to a forensic analyst: find the holes.

It obliges, gleefully. Sometimes aggressively. Sometimes it hints that it's late and I should go to bed, and I keep pushing back until crazy o'clock.

The one place we collaborate? Discussion questions. "What would make a room full of skeptical community oncologists argue with each other?" The objective is to get that guy in the back row to finally put down his phone.

Everything else is adversarial by design.

The alternative is slides that sound authoritative but are catastrophically incorrect, like about 40% of currently circulating CME content.

I didn't say that. The AI told me. I just didn't argue back.

My junior medical editor just 'corrected' me by quoting data out of context. 

Why? Because AI has the institutional memory of a goldfish. And I may as well be some stranger randomly asking it to review tumor board slide decks.

Rather than get frustrated, I started taking notes. Each error gets added to a living guideline that gets read before diving into the next project. Sources limited to loaded PDFs only? Got it. Line-by-line editing? Yup. Now, corrections get fact-checked too. And as usual, the buck stops with me.

I'm happy to say that the review cycles are gradually shortening, which is good for both of us because I'm a bit of a drama queen about errors. 

The goldfish didn't get smarter. I just started building a tank for its amnesia.

Make your notes once. Feed them in. Keep going. Your future self will feel annoyingly pleased.

It's tempting to blame the tool. But after my last CME project, I asked my AI assistant for feedback on how I work. Turns out it had notes.

My instincts were often ahead of the checks. The questions that most improved the deck came from me: "How do the endpoint definitions differ?" "Why does this data look so complicated, and where's the upside?" "Who's missing from these trials?" Clinical judgment isn't something you hand off.

I was at my best when I was skeptical. Every time I pushed back with "are you sure?" or "you've told me two different things," the work got sharper. AI sounds equally confident whether it's right or wrong. So does my GPS, before telling me to turn into a lake.

Things slipped when the pace picked up. The misses came near deadlines, especially in corrections that sounded clean. So I built a mandatory line-by-line final audit into every project.

The final calls were mine. I didn't follow every suggestion. Weighing the advice and deciding is part of the job, and it's my name on the invoice.

AI is a fast, tireless second pair of eyes. The judgment is still mine, and my gut is worth trusting. When something feels off, it usually is.

Have you ever asked your tools what they've learned about how you work?

 #AI #CME #MedEd #MedComms

What happens if you hand an AI a stack of recent EGFR-mutant NSCLC abstracts and ask for a CME deck? Probably something like this:

The AI notices that ivonescimab and pembrolizumab both hit PD-1. It concludes they're basically the same drug.

They are not the same drug.

Slide 7 cites HARMONi-A to argue that pembrolizumab plus chemo is a solid option after EGFR-TKI progression.

Slide 12 cites KEYNOTE-789, where pembrolizumab plus chemo after TKI failure missed its PFS and OS endpoints.

Slide 19 cites osimertinib resistance data to support immunotherapy after progression. The data are about MET amplification and small-cell transformation. Neither is an indication for pembrolizumab.

No slide mentions what happens when osimertinib follows a recent checkpoint inhibitor. (Pneumonitis. Pneumonitis is what happens.)

By slide 23, the AI has synthesized two years of the field into the medical equivalent of a man arguing with himself in a parking lot.

The peer reviewer asks whether the learning objectives are "intentionally Socratic."

The lesson: AI reads the literature the way a golden retriever reads Kant. Tremendous enthusiasm. Genuinely no idea what's happening. Occasionally sits on something important.

AI can draft a deck in an afternoon. Catching slide 7 still takes someone who knows a PD-1/VEGF bispecific isn't pembrolizumab with extra steps.

The parking lot guy is still out there, though.

Chemo-triplet evidence is strongest for de novo & high-volume disease. Ditto for #PSMAddition, with encouraging data in subgroups where chemo data are thinner. How will this inform your practice?

In PSMA+ mHSPC, Pluvicto triplet or chemo triplet first?

No head-to-head data. 

PSMAddition = ADT + ARPI ± Lu-PSMA-617
PEACE-1/ARASENS = ADT + docetaxel ± ARPI 

The chemo-triplet OS story is mature; the Pluvicto story is compelling, but OS is still maturing.

Do you treat the biology now, or reserve for later?

Rash is a key daraxonrasib toxicity despite recommended upfront tetracycline + topical steroid (adherence not specified). COCOON's bundle (ceramide barrier, 12 wks not 8, scalp care) cut grade ≥2 non-paronychia derm AEs 46%. Cross-trial comparisons are inherently flawed, and ami-laz isn’t purely pathway-driven. Dr. Shubham Pant, you’ve been discussing this; has a COCOON-style approach come up? #PancreaticCancer #MedicalOncology #SupportiveCare

With 2L daraxonrasib doubling mOS vs chemo for mPDAC in RASolute 302 (now under FDA review), focus is already shifting towards 1L (RASolute 303) and even adjuvant use (RASolute 304). In parallel, novel agents are advancing to personalize therapy for KRAS G12D and MTAP loss.

With benefit still measured in months and oncology teams pivoting to address toxicities, I'm looking forward to seeing where the research takes us!
